newsitem.title: JAPAN: At 50, N.Korea news wire vows no end to propaganda.
newsitem.headline: At 50, N.Korea news wire vows no end to propaganda.

text.p: North Korea's official news agency and propaganda organ marked its 50th anniversary on Thursday with a pledge to continue unstinting praise for leader Kim Jong-il and his late father and national founder, Kim Il-sung.

"The 50 years of Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) are a proud history in which it has fully played its role as a powerful ideological weapon for propagandising the greatness of comrade Kim Il-sung and comrade Kim Jong-il," the agency said in a report monitored in Tokyo.

"KCNA has developed to be an authoritative news agency equipped with able journalists faithful to the (Korean Workers') Party and the leader and with modern facilities and material and technical foundations," a KCNA reporter was quoted as telling a gathering in Pyongyang on Wednesday.

The reporter exhorted KCNA staff, who were decorated with medals, "to continue information and propaganda activities to see all the people venerating comrade Kim Il-sung as the eternal leader of the Korean revolution and conduct propaganda of the respected general Kim Jong-il's greatness intensively".
Kim Il-sung, who founded the KCNA, died in July 1994.
His son, Kim Jong-il, is believed to have assumed his father's duties at the helm of the country of 20 million people but has not officially taken the title of state president or ruling party chief.
To outsiders, KCNA appears to be the unremittingly shrill voice of the world's last Stalinist state and an echo of the most bitter language of the Cold War.

A typical day's file on KCNA mixes articles praising the exploits of the Kims and statements from obscure African leftist groups supporting Pyongyang's policies with stories describing the United States as "imperialist warmaniacs" and South Korean President Kim Young-sam and his government as "heinous gangsters" and "fascist tyrants".

For outside analysts of North Korea, however, KCNA is a barometer of inter-Korean relations and one of only two ways to monitor official statements of a highly secretive state which has few international contacts and seldom offers access to outside journalists.

The service carries policy statements from North Korea's foreign ministry that in recent years have served as the country's first answer to tense diplomatic questions such as its alleged nuclear weapons programme or peace offers by the United States and South Korea.
The other source of official North Korean information, Radio Pyongyang, offers fare similar to KCNA in Korean, Japanese, English and other languages.

South Korea, still technically at war with North Korea since an armistice ended fighting in 1953, bans distribution of KCNA as information benefiting North Korea and violators can be jailed for up to seven years.
